name: pomodoro
title: A Pomodoro timer in the terminal
pitch: 25 minutes of work, 5 minutes of break: a timer you'll actually use while you study. It starts with two printf and a sleep, and grows into a tool that counts your sessions and survives Ctrl+C.

steps.done: the two messages come 5 seconds apart.
steps.why: Your first C program that waits. `-Wall` turns on the compiler's warnings: read them, they catch mistakes before you run anything.

steps.do: Show a countdown that updates on the same line instead of filling the screen.
steps.done: the seconds go down on one line.
steps.hint: `\r` sends the cursor back to the start of the line. `fflush(stdout)` makes it show right away.
steps.why: Output is buffered: C waits for a full line before showing it. `fflush` forces it out, and you'll meet buffering again in files and pipes.

steps.do: Show the time as minutes and seconds, like 24:59.
steps.hint: Integer division `/` gives the minutes, the remainder `%` gives the seconds; `%02d` pads with a zero.
steps.why: `/` and `%` on integers are a pair you'll use for clocks, grids and pages. `%02d` keeps 25:05 from becoming 25:5.

steps.do: Beep or show a clear message when the time is up.
steps.done: you notice the end without watching the screen.
steps.hint: Printing `\a` makes the terminal beep (if its bell is on).
steps.why: A timer is only useful if it gets your attention. `\a` is an old control character every terminal knows.

steps.do: Chain the cycle: 25 minutes of work, 5 of break, 4 times, then a long break of 15 minutes.
steps.done: the timer goes through the whole cycle by itself (test it with seconds instead of minutes).
steps.hint: A function `countdown(seconds, label)` and a `for` loop around it.
steps.why: Testing with seconds instead of minutes is a real technique: make the slow thing fast while you check the logic.

steps.do: Take the durations from the command line, with sensible defaults: `./pomodoro 25 5`.
steps.done: `./pomodoro 1 1` runs one-minute periods, and a word instead of a number prints how to use it.
steps.hint: `int main(int argc, char *argv[])`, and `strtol` to read numbers (it tells you where the number stopped).
steps.why: `atoi("abc")` silently returns 0. `strtol` lets you detect bad input, which is why careful C code prefers it.

steps.do: Save each finished work session (date and time) in a file.
steps.done: the file grows by one line per session.
steps.hint: `fopen(path, "a")` opens for appending; `time()`, `localtime()` and `strftime()` format the date.
steps.why: "a" adds to the end without erasing what's there. Mixing up "w" and "a" is a classic way to lose a history file.

steps.do: Add `./pomodoro stats` to print how many sessions you did today and this week.
steps.hint: Read the file line by line with `fgets`, and compare the date at the start of each line.
steps.why: Reading back what your program wrote closes the loop: the file format you chose earlier now decides how easy this step is.

steps.do: Handle Ctrl+C: save the unfinished session as stopped instead of losing it.
steps.done: Ctrl+C prints a message and the file says "stopped".
steps.hint: `signal(SIGINT, handler)`. Inside the handler, only set a flag (`volatile sig_atomic_t`); act on it in your loop.
steps.why: Signals interrupt your program at any moment. Doing little in the handler and the real work in the loop is the safe pattern.

steps.do: Optional: pause with a key, or a desktop notification with notify-send.
steps.done: the pause stops the countdown and it starts again where it was.
steps.hint: `system("notify-send …")` is the quick way. A pause key needs the terminal in raw mode (termios).
steps.why: Calling another program from yours is often the quickest way to add a feature.
